He Mapi Nā Tātou, Mō Tātou: Part 2 — Create your own data. A map by you, controlled by you.

Kia ora e te whānau.

This is Part 2 of our hands-on wānanga showing you how to build your own hapū GIS — this time creating your own data to map your whenua, taonga, and sites of significance using free tools on your own computer. All data stays offline under your control — tō mapi, tō kōrero, tō rangatiratanga.

What you’ll learn
 ✅ Create new layers (points, lines, areas) for pā, urupā, mahinga kai, wāhi tino hira
 ✅ Record kōrero/attributes for each site (names, descriptions, significance)
 ✅ Style and label features so your maps are clear for whānau/trust use
 ✅ Export clean, printable PDFs/images to share
 ✅ Tips for organising and protecting your data locally (no cloud logins)
New to GIS? He pai – no prior experience needed. We go step-by-step and provide template layers to help you start faster.

Resources & downloads
 🔗 Wānanga resources: https://matawhenua.com
 🔗 LINZ Data Service: https://data.linz.govt.nz
 🔗 Download the starter GIS kete (Aug 2025): https://data.matawhenua.com/Matawhenua_ProjectData_Aug2025.zip
 🔗 Advanced GIS data collection: https://data.matawhenua.com/data.zip

Missed Part 1? Watch the August session in the Ngā Poutama MataWhenua playlist on our channel. Look out soon for part 3!

Sharemilking & Contract Milking Opportunities now available with Pāmu

At Pāmu, we’re growing the next generation of New Zealand farmers. As one of the country’s largest and most progressive farming companies, we offer career pathways in dairy farming designed for ambitious individuals ready to take the next step. For the 2026–2027 season, we’re excited to offer four dairy farms through contract milking, lower-order sharemilking, or herd-owning sharemilking. These opportunities are a chance to build equity, gain leadership experience, and work towards farm ownership—all while learning sustainable farming practices and innovative agricultural solutions.

Take your dairy farming career to the next level with Pāmu. Apply today: https://www.pamunewzealand.com/careers/sharemilking-and-contract-milking-2

Author interview: Khadro Mohamed

Before the Winter Ends by Khadro Mohamed is a deep and poignant work that spans Somalia, Egypt, and Aotearoa New Zealand. It explores a mother–son relationship and offers a stark portrayal of how past grief can shape a family. The book is destined to become a must-read and one of the most vital fiction releases of the year.
The book is a powerful, exploration of inter – generational grief and loss written with compassion in beautiful lyrical prose. Making Before the Winter Ends a compelling and highly readable book.  
About the author 
Khadro Mohamed is a writer and poet from Te Whanganui-a-Tara, Wellington. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from Te Herenga Waka—Victoria University of Wellington. Khadro Mohamed burst onto the literary scene with her exceptional collection of poetry, We’re All Made of Lightning, which quickly gained rave reviews and went on to win the Jessie Mackay Prize for the Best First Book of Poetry at the 2023 Ockham New Zealand Book Awards. Her much-anticipated first novel, Before the Winter Ends, is now here.

Update from Paula Tesoriero, CE at Ministry of Disabled People - Whaikaha (October 2025)

In our October update, our Chief Executive reflects on our progress over the past year.

To have our updates delivered straight to your inbox, please visit www.whaikaha.govt.nz/newsletter-sign-up

Visual description: CE Paula Tesoriero (short blonde hair) speaks to the camera while wearing a black and white top. She stands next to an NZSL interpreter (with short, dark hair and a beard), who wears a black shirt. They stand in front of a purple Whaikaha banner.

Video transcript:
Ngā mihi nui, kia koutou katoa. Ko Paula Tesoriero tōku ingoa. My name is Paula and I'm the Chief Executive of the Ministry of Disabled People - Whaikaha. My sign name is this, which is 2 fists moving in a forward direction like a bicycle. 

It’s been a big year, and I’m excited to bring you regular updates as we near our first birthday as a standalone government agency. We’ve built strong foundations and worked together to help achieve our vision of disabled people thriving in New Zealand. 
A key milestone has been refreshing the New Zealand Disability Strategy, focusing on health, housing, justice, education, and employment – alongside a renewed vision and principles section. 

We formed working groups, including people with lived disability experience, government officials, and sector experts, to develop actions for each priority area.
Over 900 people joined more than 40 consultation sessions, and your voices have shaped our direction—thank you! I look forward to the release of the final strategy in early December.

Alongside the New Zealand Sign Language Board, we’ve updated the New Zealand Sign Language Strategy to address ongoing barriers faced by Deaf people and Turi Māori. The final strategy, aimed at enabling full participation, will be launched in November.
In August, we launched a paid summer internship for final-year disabled students and recent graduates, spanning 11 government agencies. I can’t wait to meet the interns who begin in November.

In July, we launched Whaimana – Support My Decisions, a website offering practical tools and examples to help people make informed choices. Developed with input from the disability sector, it has received positive feedback and will continue to grow.

We’ve also:
• supported agencies to implement the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recommendations
• contributed to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care response
• released the National Pacific Disability Approach
• expanded access to disability data, evidence, and insights
• made progress on our Accessibility Work Programme, including strengthening the Alternate Formats Service, and inviting expressions of interest for our new Accessibility Advisory Group.
We’re making sure essential government information that disabled people told us need translating into alternate formats. We're beginning with details on Work and Income benefits, MSD processes, and complaints, with more resources to follow.
We're increasing public understanding of disability issues by collaborating with the parking sector to improve mobility parking enforcement and promoting awareness of disability assist dog access rights. Building strong relationships with the disability community and related organisations remains a key focus.
You can also check out our recently released annual report, which highlights our first year of progress as a standalone department

I’m grateful for the opportunity to hear people’s views and experiences first-hand. These conversations continue to shape our priorities.

Disabled people still face many barriers, but as we approach our first anniversary on the 1st of December, I’m proud of what we’ve achieved together to create meaningful change. There is much more to be done.

Ngā mihi nui, kia koutou katoa.

Paula Tesoriero thanks the NZ public for their feedback

In this video, Whaikaha CEO Paula Tesoriero (with an NZSL interpreter) shares her thanks to everyone who gave feedback on the draft New Zealand Disability Strategy. They speak directly to the camera against a grey wall.

Transcript:

Tēnā koutou katoa, talofa lava, mālō e lelei, bula vinaka, warm Pacific greetings.     

My name is Paula, I’m the Chief Executive of the Ministry of Disabled People - Whaikaha.  

My sign name is this (demonstrates move), which is 2 fists moving in a forward direction like a bicycle. 

I want to say a big thank you, he mihi nui, to everyone who took part in the public consultation on the draft New Zealand Disability Strategy. 

We received more than 550 submissions, we met with over 900 people, and I know a number of you also held your own feedback sessions, and provided your feedback.

I was fortunate enough to attend a number of the hui, and had the opportunity to listen first-hand to what you thought of the strategy.

Thank you again, and I look forward to sharing the final strategy with you later this year. 

Nga mihi nui, kia koutou katoa.
